A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SonicSim/SonicSet research. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations, and appendices are readable and can be matched despite reorganization.

before.justification: Sections 4–5 and Tables 2–6 report original experiments with 11 speech separation and nine speech enhancement models on synthetic and real-world recordings.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds original environmental-factor results and HumanSEP/HumanENH evaluations in Tables 7–8 and 10–11.

M1.justification: The Habitat-sim simulation, trajectory-based RIR convolution and interpolation, microphone configurations, and benchmark training objectives remain. More explicit interpolation and microphone-array descriptions document the existing procedure without establishing an implemented method change.

E1.justification: v2 adds HumanSEP and HumanENH, each described as recordings of 16 speakers across six scenarios, extending evaluation to directly recorded human speech for both tasks. Existing datasets remain; RealSEP names the previously reported five-hour playback-based separation dataset rather than introducing another dataset.

E2.justification: Tables 2–6 retain the same 11 separation and nine enhancement comparators and the same training-dataset comparison groups. The new human-recording evaluations reuse these comparators, while environmental tests use subsets of existing models.

E3.justification: v2 adds NISQA evaluation across both tasks and MOS Overall reporting for separation. New protocols include controlled environmental manipulations using 300 LibriSpeech files and human-recording evaluations with specified sentence lengths, noise, and speaker overlap. Most original training settings match v1's appendices; their appearance in new main-text implementation sections is largely relocation.

E4.justification: New Appendix A tests obstacles, cylindrical versus cuboid rooms, and presence versus absence of material information while controlling source and microphone positions. Tables 7–8 report SDR and WER for two separation and two enhancement models. v1 contains no equivalent environmental-factor ablations.

E5.justification: Neither version reports seed counts, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Results remain point estimates; the horizontal table bars represent value magnitudes rather than uncertainty.

E6.justification: v2 adds quality-metric results and four experimental tables while retaining existing numerical entries in Tables 2–5. Several Table 6 values change, including Fast-FullSubNet's musical-noise SDR from 11.24 to 11.92. New HumanENH results show lower WER but lower NISQA for SonicSet training than DNS Challenge training across all nine models.

T1.justification: Section 3.2.2 newly specifies a distance-ratio interpolation weight and mathematical signal construction that v1 described procedurally; existing task definitions and loss equations remain unchanged. The new weight evaluates from 1 to 0 between the stated endpoints, contradicting the accompanying claim that it progresses from 0 to 1.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contributions: customizable moving-source simulation, the SonicSet benchmark, and improved real-world generalization from SonicSet training. Additional evaluations support these existing claims without redefining their scope.

C2.justification: v2 clarifies that imported scene geometry cannot be edited and adds environmental-sensitivity interpretations, deployment tradeoffs, and possible speech-artifact explanations in Appendices A, D.7, and E.5. The central realism/generalization interpretation and the original limitation concerning incomplete 3D scenes remain.

D1.justification: New disclosures include the ShortestPath API, microphone-array coordinate construction, an example generator configuration, and HumanSEP/HumanENH recording details. Much of the newly prominent training documentation already appeared in v1's appendices. The enhancement-code footnote changes from a GitHub repository to an anonymous repository.

R1.justification: v2 adds Slaney et al. and Freeland et al. for interpolation and Mittag et al. for NISQA, while removing several introductory and framework references. The substantive positioning against existing datasets and acoustic simulators remains.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related-work passages, and dataset-construction explanation are substantially rewritten or condensed. Implementation details become main-text subsections, appendix material is reorganized, and the existing real-world separation dataset receives the name RealSEP. These changes extend beyond isolated copyediting.

P2.justification: v2 adds four experimental tables and expands Tables 2–6 with additional metric columns, changing their density and formatting. Existing Figures 1–6 and the dataset-statistics table are retained and repositioned, and a generator-configuration listing is added alongside the retained metadata example.

improvement.justification: The human-speech evaluations and environmental-factor tests provide useful additional checks of real-world applicability, while new configuration and recording details improve reproducibility. These benefits are tempered by the unexplained recognition-versus-NISQA tradeoff in the enhancement results and the newly inconsistent interpolation formula in Section 3.2.2. Overall, the evidence becomes more informative, but unresolved interpretation and correctness issues limit the quality gain.
